subtopic: CALL FOR PROVISION OF SERVICE TO NEW HOME OWNERS
CALL FOR PROVISION OF SERVICE TO NEW HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the recent housing construction boom in Kitchener and Waterloo has created a class of home owners who have fallen victim to Canada Post's freeze on extending home delivery. This freeze applies to new subdivisions and even to new homes recently added to streets which have always received home delivery.
Some of these homeowners must now use neighbourhood group boxes. Others, lacking even this necessity, must drive to their nearest post office and wait in long lines at inconvenient hours, often during work, in order to collect their mail. Furthermore, I am told that Canada Post proposes to continue this trend as cost saving measure.
While the end may be laudable, the means is unjustifiable. Perhaps a modest reduction in petty grievances, days absent, and strike activity amongst Canada Post personnel, coupled with an increase in their efficiency and productivity, would achieve the same end without forfeiting service. Therefore I call upon the Government to ensure that Canada Post provides all new home owners with the same level of service presently accorded their fellow taxpayers elsewhere.
Let me add that I welcome the Marchment Committee's report on the mandate and productivity of Canada Post Corporation. I trust that this report will act as an impetus for Canada Post to work toward a level of service with which its Canadian consumers can be satisfied and in which its employees can take pride.

FIELD HOCKEY-REPORTED CANCELLATION OF ARTIFICIAL TURF FACILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, only a few weeks ago the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport (Mr. Jelinek) blatantly interfered in the internal affairs of the National Women's Field Hockey Association over the selection of its national coach. The incident has left many serious and permanent scars. Now the Minister has dealt another more serious blow to the field hockey movement.
It has been learned that the Conservative Government will not honour a $1.3 million commitment made by the previous Liberal Government toward the establishment of an artificial turf installation at the University of British Columbia. This would have provided amateur sports with a permanent and much needed training centre. The previous Government was prepared to recognize the need for such a world class facility. The Conservative Government, however, seems to be completely indifferent. To make matters worse, on November 7, over CBC radio, the Minister promised to keep all sports commitments made by the previous Government.
As a result of Tory double-talk, Canada was forced to relinquish the hosting of the women's World Cup tournament scheduled to take place in Vancouver next year. This is a serious embarrassment in the eyes of the international sports community. In addition, of course, our amateur athletes will lose out on a very necessary and competent training centre. 1 therefore call upon that Government and that Minister to honour the former Government's financial commitment and be sensitive to the deficiency of such facilities available to our amateur sports and amateur athletes across the country.

subsubtopic: CROP DISASTER ASSISTANCE-STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would just like to begin by saying that in keeping with this Government's long-standing commitment to support and give assistance to the agricultural industry across this country, it gives me a great deal of pleasure today to announce the federal Government's decision to commit up to $150 million toward
Statements by Ministers
the Crop Disaster Assistance Program in order to assist crop producers in the southern Prairies and the Peace River region.

subsubtopic: CROP DISASTER ASSISTANCE-STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CROP DISASTER ASSISTANCE-STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
This program will complement the efforts being made by the provincial Governments of British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba to relieve the financial crisis in western Canadian agriculture.
Our plan is to make a yield deficiency payment to farmers in the areas where cumulative crop losses, primarily due to drought, have been the worst over the past three years. These areas would be determined based on crop insurance records and county or rural municipality yield records. We expect that some 30,000 farmers would be eligible for a share of this assistance. Administrative details, including where farmers can get application forms, will be announced in the very near future. I can assure Hon. Members that these farmers will be dealt with with dispatch.
Of the federal Government's $150 million contribution, $95 million will be provided this fall and the remaining $55 million will be paid in April in time for next year's seeding.
As Hon. Members of the House know, our Government has been and continues to be extremely concerned about the impact of successive droughts on prairie grain and livestock farmers. In fact, in the fall of 1984, we provided a $30 million federal contribution to help livestock producers retain their breeding herds over the winter. Subsequent to that, we made a $123 million final payment under the Western Grain Stabilization Plan. In addition, we amended the Western Grain Stabilization Act in order to make an interim payment prior to seeding this spring and that contribution amounted to $450 million.
Recently, my colleague, the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer), made an announcement of the final payment under the Act of an additional $72 million. Incidentally, those cheques are now in the hands of western farmers.
We again responded to the plight of the prairie livestock producers with a $48 million federal drought assistance package announced in August. We recently announced interest free cash advances of up to $3,000 per producer to assist in drying tough or damp grain. As well, the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board earlier indicated we would be prepared to make cash advances for unharvested crops, and today I want to assure all farmers that these advances will in fact be offered to those who are unable to harvest their grain.
While the crop insurance under the Western Grain Stabilization Program has paid out nearly $2 billion in the past two crop years, the successive years of drought, severe grasshopper infestations, poor harvest weather and low commodity prices have left a great many farmers with insufficient cash flow to meet their expenses and to continue to produce crops. The $150 million program we are announcing today will provide immediate relief and we will continue our efforts to develop a long term approach to emergency funding.
8870

November 27, 1985

There is no question about the fact that there are many western farmers, good farmers, who, through no fault of their own, need special assistance measures at this time. That is what we are providing today. But we all appreciate that ad hoc measures and programs are not an ideal solution. It is disruptive to producers to live with the uncertainty of not knowing what back-up assistance they will receive when natural disasters occur. Nor is it easy for the federal Government to take on substantial new financial commitments which have not been previously budgeted. That is why we are viewing the Crop Disaster Assistance Program as a field test for a permanent emergency assistance program which could be offered to farmers as a complement or extension to the current Crop Insurance Program. I believe it is incumbent on us to revise the Crop Insurance Program to allow producers some additional protection. We hope to be able to work out these details with the provinces in time for the 1986 crop year.
The federal Government now contributes over $200 million annually to the Crop Insurance Program across Canada and I believe about $160 million of that is directed to western Canada.
I would also at this time like to thank my colleague, the Hon. Member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson), the Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister-

I believe all Hon. Members of this House recognize the personal commitment and, indeed, without exaggeration, the hundreds of man-hours which the Hon. Member for Assiniboia dedicated to this work. The Crop Disaster Assistance Program I am announcing today has been made possible in no small measure by the Hon. Member's unceasing efforts to assist western farmers.
This program should help farmers in the drought area overcome the economic hardship which prolonged periods of drought have created. This is important to all Canadians since prairie grain and oilseed production is worth about $7.5 billion a year at the farm gate and provides the base for an estimated $35 billion a year in economic activity. This tremendous agricultural resource must be protected during these difficult times so that it may continue to enrich Canadians for generations to come.

subsubtopic: CROP DISASTER ASSISTANCE-STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to see that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) had the hallelujah chorus lined up behind him this afternoon as he made his announcement. We are pleased to see that the Minister finally made the announcement. We wish that he had made it back on September 10 when this House commenced
its fall sitting because the situation on the Prairies was desperate. That has been apparent since mid-July. 1 know the Minister visited Assiniboia and other places, as did I and many other Members of this House back in July. We saw a crop three or four inches high and absolutely devoid of any seed. We have seen the situation exacerbated over the fall months with young farmers losing their farms and being refused welfare. We are also glad that he reversed himself on the position he took on December 19, 1984 when he said that never again would a Conservative Government make a payment of this type for crop disaster. However, this decision could just as easily have been made in early September. The cheques could have been in the farmers' hands by now. Given that the mechanics involved in paying this money, the application forms and the criteria, have not even been worked out, very few payments will be made before January of next year. At that, only about two-thirds of the payment will be made, with the rest being paid next May or later on.
Some may think that an announcement of $150 million for crop disaster assistance in western Canada is a great deal of money. However, when we look at the disaster itself involving $2 billion to $3 billion, it does not look very large. We are dealing here with a massive disaster. In Saskatchewan alone it is estimated that 8.2 million acres were affected by severe drought, with 6.3 million acres less severely affected, and some
14,000	farmers severely affected. As one of the people from the Wheat Pool said, this seems to be less than a token gesture because, unfortunately, the Minister has not announced what the maximum benefit will be. It is probably so small that he was afraid to put it in the announcement because of the derision he would face from the thousands of farmers facing the most serious financial difficulty in the history of this country.
Using the Minister's own figures of 30,000 farmers who will benefit, and assuming that the average farm is 1,000 acres, we come up with a figure of $5 per acre. That is about what it costs to spray one application of pesticide to control the grasshoppers which infected many of these areas last summer. Some farmers had to make two or three applications and even then lost their crop because of the drought. Compare this amount of $5 per acre average to the amount recommended by the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool which represents some 60,000 farmers. They recommended a maximum of $50 per acre or 10 times what the Minister appears to have offered today. Compare the amount the Government was prepared to spend with the bank failures which has cost us at least $1 billion. Compare this amount offered today with the assistance provided by the Province of Alberta, a total of $800 million this year. Last weekend that province announced a special program involving $200 million to assist these people. However, the federal Minister announces today immediate assistance of $95 million, or less than half, with additional funding next spring of $55 million. Obviously this, when put in its true perspective, is incredibly small.
The Minister spent most of his time today talking about crop insurance and western grain stabilization payments which
November 27, 1985

had been made. I appreciate his applauding these programs which were put in place by a Liberal Government, but these are insurance programs. You pay your premium and if you have a loss, you get the benefit. Therefore, he should not be talking about these programs as if they involved some benevolence on the part of the Government itself.
The Minister also paid great tribute to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister, the Hon. Member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson), for all the work he has done. 1 wish the Parliamentary Secretary would table his report. I cannot believe that he recommended this level of assistance. I am sure it must have been two or three times this amount, and to be paid immediately, not in January or May or whenever.
In light of falling land prices, low commodity prices, international predatory pricing by the EEC and the United States, there is great concern in western Canada about the Government's commitment to agriculture. This statement today, although providing some small relief, will not lift that concern.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this announcement today finally lets farmers in western Canada know where they stand with this Government. The statement is nine pages long, but the Minister said it all in the first line. He is saying that his Government has now decided to commit up to $150 million towards crop disaster relief in the drought affected areas of western Canada. The rest tells us nothing. He says the program complements the efforts made by the provincial Government, but I think that is what a lot of producers are going to be wondering and worrying about.
The political attitude that the Minister seems to be taking is borrowed to some extent from that of the first Prime Minister of this country who was called colloquially "Old Tomorrow". Our "New Tomorrow" works by delay, delay, delay. This is a sort of follow-up on an infamous politician from my Province of Saskatchewan whose call words are deny, deny, deny. He is providing bits of policy as he goes along with a peekaboo approach to agricultural policy. Even though the Member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson) began his consultations on August 9, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) delayed making any announcement on a cattle payment until after the provinces had acted. Saskatchewan residents will recall that a week later the Government of Saskatchewan said that there would be $60 per head available to people who kept their cows over the winter. The federal Government then announced a $30 payment, which came very close to what the group bargaining on behalf of farmers had asked for. They had asked for $100 a head and everyone felt reasonably good about having achieved close to 90 per cent success. They then discovered that the $30 was not additional to the provincial program but was simply complementary to it, and it was eaten up by the provincial Government on the way through the delivery system as the full $30 stayed in provincial hands.

The Minister mentioned something about the PFRA. That was one of the things he did not mention in his nine-page statement. Perhaps he is going to supplement that, too, and there will be a policy statement in coming weeks about the PFRA or the PFAA.
The delay has allowed the Minister to follow the same route as he took with the cattle payment. He waited so long that the provinces started to put forward acreage proposals of their own. In Saskatchewan there has been a proposal of $25 per acre and of a loan at 6 per cent over three years for up to 1,200 acres. I am not sure whether some of this money will be used to pay the cost of that. That is not clear. I hope the Minister will clarify that when he leaves the Chamber. The rules of the House no longer permit us to get such answers.
On page 6 of his statement the Minister went to great pains to point out why he backed off from his position of last December 21 when he made a pay-out to farmers in northeastern Saskatchewan who had been flooded. He said at that time that that would be the last of the ad hoc programs. He said that after December 21, 1984, crop insurance would be expected to cover these types of things and that if producers did not have crop insurance they would not be covered. At least he saw the problem with that when faced with a disaster such as that

November 27, 1985
Statements by Ministers
which occurred in southern Saskatchewan and Alberta this year and he has backed off, to a very small extend, and has announced another ad hoc program. Elowever, listen to the way he describes it. He said: "It is disruptive to producers to live with the uncertainty of not knowing what back-up assistance they will receive when natural disasters befall them". That is very true. He continues: "Nor is it easy for the federal Government to take on substantial new commitments that have not been previously budgeted". Substantial new commitments? One hundred and fifty million dollars is a substantial amount of money, but not compared to the substantial commitments we made to the banks or compared to some of the tax remissions we gave oil companies. In those cases decisions were made over a weekend to spend billions of dollars, yet farmers waited three and a half months to get $150 million.

speakeroldname: Hon. Frank Oberle (Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: NATIONAL RESEARCH COUNCIL-STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF STATE FOR SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure today, as Minister of State for Science and Technology, to table the new long-range plan of the National Research Council of Canada called A Practical Perspective. This plan began to take shape under the direction of my predecessor, the Hon. Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) after last November's economic statement and took further direction from the full Budget of last May.
The NRC is the Government of Canada's principal agency for new research and development. Over the years it has adapted well to Canada's R and D needs. Today A Practical Perspective details the NRC's adjustment to our most pressing problems. We all know of the huge national debt and unemployment in all sectors. The country needs economic stimulus which creates jobs and I believe that a wise use of scarce resources in the science and technology fields holds the best promise for future growth and stability in the job market.
Unfortunately, we now find ourselves in a squeeze. Just when we need to develop new technologies we also need to limit our spending. Unless the Government keeps to its own Budget, it may worsen the very problems it tries to solve. We must solve our R and D problems with brain power since we cannot solve them through brute financial force. The National Research Council already knows this. A Practical Perspective is a deliberate reorientation by the NRC and it is consonant with government policy. It has new ideas and new directions, but none require a budget over that which has already been considered by Cabinet. The plan has my support and, I am sure, that of my colleagues in Cabinet.
Over the next year the NRC will increase its work in generic research, which work has practical applications in more than a single sector. The NRC will increase its focus on technology
transfer and diffusion, an area in which the NRC already leads the nation's research organizations. Only last month the NRC shared the Award of Excellence Gold Medal for Technology Transfer with Lumonics Inc. Some years ago the NRC made basic breakthroughs in understanding high-powered lasers. Lumonics, now one of the world's most successful laser manufacturers, then put those basic principles to use. This followed last year's success when the NRC shared another gold medal with Sciex Inc., a Toronto-based maker of mass spectrometers.
All research and development is an exercise in risk. In fact, there is only one certainty in R and D: not performing it is the worst thing a country can do in today's environment. However, for R and D to succeed it needs more than good ideas. It must also have an established long-term scientific expertise or infrastructure. I believe that the percentage of the Gross National Product which Canada spends on R and D is far too low, but in the present tight fiscal situation we must ensure that what is spent is put to optimum use. Quality more than quantity must be our guide. I think that the country has yet to extract full value from the R and D results it has already produced. Therefore, in the short term our task is to use more effectively the resources we already have.
R and D is complicated, not only in what it studies, but in how it is done. It involves our industry, our financial and business institutions, our universities and all tiers of Government. We feel its effects in our living standard, our unemployment rate and our trade balance. R and D is so vital that it must be managed properly. This is not to say there is no more room in Canada for pure research that seeks to satisfy human curiosity. But Government research laboratories must be relevant to the industry's needs in the short term. Their programs must be sensitive to the market. The plan given to us by the National Research Council will continue to give Canada its vital base for long-term research. But for the next few years, it will put more emphasis on development and diffusion, the "D", so to speak, in R and D.
We must not aim merely at yet another stockpile of new data. Any knowledge must quickly get to those who can turn it into economic growth and prosperity. Government alone cannot and should not do all the research that this country needs. However, we do want to create a climate that favours someone doing it. To create this climate, Government must find the right mix of markets, basic knowledge, locale, national needs, and most important, people. It should identify opportunities for Canada in emerging research fields. It should get Canada into the new technologies as early as possible and so pave the way for industry later to reap advantages.
As an example, let me mention Canadarm. None of its spectacular success would have been possible unless the National Research Council had a basis of expertise and had already proven able to manage advanced aerospace projects. NRC is now seeing to it that Canadarm technology finds wider use on earth, in such practical fields as machine visions
November 27, 1985

and robotics. This one advanced technology may one day let us venture safely not just into space, but beneath the seas and mountains, into nuclear reactors and toward next decade's automated factories as well. The money we invested in Canad-arm will certainly come back to us greatly multiplied over the next 20 years.
The same pay-off also happens elsewhere. Government investment in telecommunications and satellite development has put Canada on the leading edge of these technologies. Our space industry has found a lucrative niche in international markets. In fact, it sells more than its national Government spends on its entire space program, a claim that few nations can make.
The Government will do more than encourage and sustain R and D; however, we will perform R and D directly, ourselves. Our Government laboratories exist to do long-term research on Canada's national priorities. This long-term work is a kind of unseen wealth. With it in our national bank account, Canada has the basis to exploit lucrative new technologies as they appear on the horizon and will not have to start from scratch each time.
In turn, the National Research Council is indispensable to Canada's long-term R and D. It covers many disciplines and research approaches from hard technology transfer to the curiosity that gives rise to new discoveries. Some work represents both fields. For example, current NRC research in a field called "micro-propagation of conifers" promises to give us forests full of "alpha trees" that are straight, tall, healthy, quick-growing, and resistant to threats as diverse as insects and acid rain-a concern that is dear to our hearts.
There are many other major programs being planned or already under way at the National Research Council. One of these will make it easier for us to live and work in our cold oceans. Another will explore the powerful new techniques called biotechnology. Yet another will uncover useful new materials and ways of using them. The list goes on. The National Research Council laboratories are there for the nation; for business people to test products and for Government, university and industrial researchers to unlock the doors of new goods and services. Many NRC laboratories are there because they would be too costly for any single company to build and maintain. However, once in place for every company in Canada, they have proven indispensable.
Another aspect of R and D that is sometimes taken for granted is up-to-date scientific and technical information. The National Research Council distributes this to all Canadians through its national science library, because technical information cannot give full value until it is in the hands of those who can apply it. The idea holds true for every other aspect of R and D as well. It is at the centre of the National Research Council's new plan. This is why the NRC has recently built up the programs of its industry development office. The strength and effectiveness of these programs comes from the full resources of the NRC's hundreds of scientific and technical personnel. As Canadian corporations know, these programs deliver not just the latest technology but help in funding
Statements by Ministers
in-house research projects as well. The National Research Council's industrial programs offer advice on problems from small-scale production lines to the largest projects in our country.
The programs work because people can reach them. There are now over 160 NRC technology advisers in major centres in our country. Each adviser puts industrial clients in touch with the full range of federal programs and services. Each can approve most industry assistance projects with minimum delay. Over the next two years, the National Research Council will broaden and improve these successful programs. Special funds will cover the cost of studies to measure how well a proposed product might do and how best to market it. Through these programs, as well as its actual research, the National Research Council will reach every technical and business audience in Canada. It will lead and co-ordinate the effort of Canadian R and D, building the team spirit that is vital to our success.
Leadership is now the most challenging task for Canadian R and D, but also offers the greatest rewards. It involves bringing together those who actually do R and D; the universities, the provincial research organizations, the federal laboratories and industry. It must include the users and the supporters of research and development; the policy makers, the venture capitalists and other investors, the business managers, the whole Canadian workforce. All these groups stand to profit from a strong national research and development program. None can afford to work in isolation from the other any longer.
Since Parliament founded the National Research Council in 1916, it has grown from 9 advisers to 3,000 scientists, technologists, managers and support staff. These men and women link many times their number in members of Canada's scientific and technical community. For example, over 100 professionals from all fields serve as members of the NRC's various associated and advisory committees. Even more people in Canada's industrial sector rely on NRC programs for financial and technical assistance.
The National Research Council will continue to build on the respect it has earned as a leader of Canada's research and development community. It will work even harder and bring together the producers and end users of the research data. The National Research Council's regional offices will be points of contact where key people can meet. The NRC will establish a Technology Assessment Office helping Canadians to keep up with new technology beyond our borders. The NRC's associate committees will let Canada's scientists, technologists and industrialists have a direct say in national R and D policy. In short, the National Research Council will continue to be the breeding ground for excellence in Canadian science, technology and commerce. This is its natural role both in history and today.
I wish to take this opportunity to congratulate the many people in the National Research Council who have served us so well over the last 70 years. Of course, I want to congratu-

November 27, 1985
Statements by Ministers
late them for the preparation of this document in helping us to achieve the objectives that we have set.
It is my pleasure to table the document from the NRC which is entitled A Practical Perspective. I ask, Mr. Speaker, that you seek unanimous consent to return to Tabling of Documents in order to permit me to table these documents under Standing Order 47(2) in both official languages.

subsubtopic: NATIONAL RESEARCH COUNCIL-STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF STATE FOR SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: NATIONAL RESEARCH COUNCIL-STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF STATE FOR SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the Minister on his appointment to this vital portfolio and to wish him well in his endeavours. I want to thank him also for the courtesy he extended to me by sending a copy of the plan and his statement yesterday which enabled me to prepare my remarks.
I might say at the outset that I know he is not responsible for the plan because it was printed before he was named Minister. I hope he will perhaps take into consideration some of my remarks today in seeking to improve the plan. [Translation]
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to comment today on the new plan for the National Research Council. It is a plan we have been expecting for some time, and it contains a number of interesting proposals with respect to innovation in Canada's private sector.

I cannot help but feel that it is the plan of an agency in trouble, an agency whose status has yet to be resolved by its political masters. Nowhere in the plan, Mr. Speaker, nor in the Minister's statement, is there a reference to the Nielsen task force and the recommendations that were tabled with the Budget last May.
The activities and recommendations of the task force and, in particular, the secretive manner in which it has conducted its work, have raised deep concerns and frustrations in the scientific community across Canada. Scientists need to have adequate resources and a positive climate in which to work. I sincerely hope that the new Minister will clear the air as soon as possible regarding the status of the Nielsen task force.
Second, when one looks at the single page in the plan devoted to funding, it is apparent that the plan can only be viewed as a plan of austerity. There is no increase in the NRC's budget in 1986, the first year of the plan and only a 2 per cent increase in 1987. Spending levels for years three, four
and five are yet to be determined. It is a five-year plan which is a two-year plan. There seems to be no provision for an increase to keep pace with inflation, which means that spending will actually decline in the next two years. This decline comes from a Government and a Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) that promised increased spending on research and development.
From where will the money come to support the new initiatives, Mr. Speaker? What will be cut? There is not a word about this either in the plan or in the Minister's statement. Where is the money for Science Place Canada in Winnipeg or for the biotechnology centre in Montreal? [Translation]
Mr. Speaker, where is the money for the Institut d'optique in Quebec City?
Today I spoke to a reporter from Quebec who told me that the project was at a standstill.

The Government, Mr. Speaker, has been playing games with Canadians. It has been talking about involving the private sector and the provinces but it has not yet put a penny on the table for these important projects.
I would like to contrast this plan with NRC's long-range plan presented in 1979. In the plan called The Urgent Investment the president stated at the time that the NRC had "an major role to play" in meeting the goal of spending 1.5 per cent of Canada's Gross National Product on research and development. The President of the NRC stated that the immediate and central target of the Council was to stimulate the technology-intensive industrial sector to increase its contribution to the gross domestic product from $20 billion at that time in 1979 to $40 billion by 1990. Exports should increase had this plan been carried out and imports reduced, with a net effect of up to $12 billion on our balance of payments. Additional employment of 650,000 jobs should result, said the President of the National Research Council in 1979. Boy, could we use those 650,000 jobs. The achievement of this target, concluded the President of the NRC, would have significant effects on some of Canada's economic problems.
To achieve this objective, the NRC's expenditures under its long-range plan in 1979 would have increased to $1.25 billion by 1990 under the preferred alternative presented by the Council. There was a second and a third alternative, albeit less ambitious than the first. The NRC observed, in particular, that the third alternative assumes the gloomy view that the economic and other objectives of the NRC long-term plan must be significantly reduced.
Under the Liberal Government, Mr. Speaker, great progress had been made in achieving the preferred objective. Expenditures in 1984-85 reached $501 million. We know what has happened since the day the Conservatives were elected. Since that election, that sorry day last September, significant cuts have been made in NRC's budget so that the Government's Estimates for spending this year, in 1985-86, are below the level of the gloomy third alternative of the previous long-range
November 27, 1985

plan. With a record like this, is it surprising that there is such widespread disappointment in the Government's record concerning research and development?
Yesterday I read that the President of MacDonald Dettwil-er, one of Canada's most important and dynamic high-tech companies, said that he would like to hear the Prime Minister make a firm statement that science and technology is important to the Government and the country. He said-and this is most important because we have heard a lot of blarney for the last number of years-that he would like the Prime Minister to put his money where his mouth is.
Another question which is unanswered in the plan or in the statement of the Minister is the budget proposal to consolidate NRC's Industrial Research Assistance Program with the innovation section of the Industrial and Regional Development Program administered by the Department of Regional and Economic Expansion. Is the responsibility for this plan to be transferred to the NRC or to the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion? If there is to be a transfer to the NRC, how much is to be transferred? Will additional resources be provided to the NRC for the basic research which supports the IRAP? There is no indication in the Minister's statement or in the plan about these vital questions.
There is nothing either about the external review proposed by the Wright task force. True, the NRC proposes an expansion of its associated committees and boards on which there are outside representatives. I do not fault the Minister for this, perhaps it is the fault of the previous Minister. However, the Minister has not said whether he agrees with the advice which the previous Minister asked for and received from the NRC, namely, that an arm's length agency should conduct an external review.
I also note that there is only one strong statement in the plan about basic research. That contrasts with the many strong statements about basic research in the original long-range plan tabled in 1979. A single page, which seems unrelated to the rest of the document, deals with basic research. On page 55 we find the heading: "One Analysis". The heading itself suggests that it does not belong, that it is not in keeping with the rest of the plan. The person who undertook the analysis for the NRC was a member of the Council, a D. J. Doyle of Doyletech Corporation. The conclusion of his study indicated the following:
-that Canada would best be served by an NRC that had greater funding and a larger proportion of its efforts devoted to long-term basic research. Doyle's argument was that a long-term commitment to basic research provides the continuity, breadth of vision, and forecasting ability that leads to the generation of new technologies. A single-minded devotion to short-term exploitation of technological knowledge imposes a restricted view.
It seems clear that Mr. Doyle disagrees with the basic orientation of the plan, namely, an increased focus on applied research. There is nothing wrong with that, as long as resources are provided for the additional applied research, as long as resources are provided for the additional efforts to be made in development, and as long as basic research does not
Statements by Ministers
suffer. The only conclusion to be reached is that basic research will suffer from the Government's emphasis upon applied research and development.
I have been warned time and time again by scientists in universities and the private sector that Canada must contribute to the general advancement of knowledge in the world, or we will be shut out by our competitors and forced to buy their discoveries on their terms, after they have taken the first steps in exploiting the commercial potential of the discoveries. This is the kind of world into which the Government is blindly leading us.

Mr. Speaker, it is highly irresponsible of the Government to leave the National Research Council more or less in limbo and fail to give it the resources it needs to carry out the urgent investments proposed in 1979.
For a year and a half, Government cutbacks and the work of the task force headed by the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) have given rise to considerable uncertainty about the future of the NRC's programs.
We must put an end to this uncertainty and do so quickly, if we want a climate that is conducive to research in Canada. [English]
This plan is nothing other than a disappointment. It does not answer many important and serious questions. It leaves a cloud hanging over the NRC. It is not the kind of bold blueprint for the future which our country desperately needs.

subsubtopic: NATIONAL RESEARCH COUNCIL-STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF STATE FOR SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I want to congratulate my long-time colleague from British Columbia on becoming the new Minister of Science and Technology. I know him well. I wish him well. I am sure he will be a very competent Minister. I am sure the House wishes him the best. In some ways I feel a little sorry for him today because he is the delivery boy for the former Minister. The statement before the House is not something upon which we can judge the present Minister. It is not a reflection of his ideas. It is a reflection of the ideas of the former Minister. He has had to come to the House with the former Minister's bad news and ideas, ideas which have seen many cut-backs in and a wrong orientation toward the NRC. I would hope-and this is my one wish for today-that the new Minister will be a better advocate of the scientific community and the aspirations of that community than was the former Minister, who underwent much criticism from scientists from one part of the country to the other. I wish him well and look forward to some innovative ideas in the future.
The most important sector in the country-and we often tend to overlook it-is the scientific sector involved in research and development. In the world of the future, what we do in terms of scientific research and development will be very important for jobs in the country, for the standard of living of our people and for the whole future of Canada.
Many years ago it was said that the muscular power and the financial power of people were important. I suggest that today

November 27, 1985
Statements by Ministers
knowledge is the most important. Knowledge is power. Countries, sectors and communities with knowledge are the ones which will have power and influence in the world of the future. That in itself is very, very important.
Today we have had the tabling of a new five-year plan for the National Research Council. It is a second five-year plan. It is a lot less comprehensive in nature and in terms of details, as anyone can see by reading through it, than the original plan of some five years or six years ago. The old plan was more detailed. We can see this from its sheer volume. It contained many more statistics, details and idealistic ideas on where we wanted to go. We have had first year and second year reports on it. The second five-year plan does not contain the same detailed information.
During the 1984 election campaign-and this is something which the new Minister understands very well-his Party and his Leader promised to double Canadian spending on research and development over the next five years. That was a doubling in five years, from 1984-85 to 1989-90. That was a promise made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), and now the Minister has the difficult mandate of fulfilling it. In the statement before us today there is no reference to that promise. Instead of a fulfillment of the particular promise, we see a cut-back in spending at the National Research Council. In year one, 1986, according to the plan, there will be a zero increase in the budget. In 1987, year two, there will be an increase of 2 per cent. This means that in 1986 because of inflation, there will be a cut-back of 4 per cent or 5 per cent. In 1987, because of an increase of only 2 per cent in spending, there will be another cut-back, since inflation is likely to be more than 2 per cent. In years three, four and five, 1988, 1989 and 1990, the increases are to be determined.
Perhaps we can hope that the Minister, in the cabinet room, carries a big stick and is able to get a bit of money out of those tightwads, the Minister responsible for finance, to finance scientific research and development as they should be financed. In that I wish him well.
Certainly the previous Minister failed. Last November, in the statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), there was a cut-back in spending of $70 million for the NRC. In fiscal year 1985-86, its budget is to be $419.1 million, whereas in 1984-85, its budget was $478.2 million.

As I said before, Mr. Speaker, during the 1984 election campaign, the Prime Minister promised to double spending on research and development in Canada. This was a very important promise involving a very important sector. However, as I said earlier, in November 1984 the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) cut $70 million from the NRC's budget. I think the science sector is so important it cannot afford budgetary cutbacks of $70 million per year.
Mr. Speaker, Canada's science sector holds the future of this country, of our young people, and of agriculture, fisheries, forestry and our natural resources. It is vitally important.
Mr. Speaker, I wish the new Minister the best of luck.
However, there have been cut-backs. The Energy Division itself which is responsible for alternative energy research has been cut, as has been the Environmental Secretariat. Also dumped was a manufacturing technology centre in Winnipeg even though the construction of the building had already begun.
The National Research Council's five-year plan does not anticipate any increase in spending because of inflation and actual roll-back over the next few years. In the five-year plan for 1980 to 1985, the first produced by the current President, Mr. Kerwin, a very large role was envisaged for the NRC in both basic and applied research.
The old five-year plan presented three funding options. The first option proposed a greatly enhanced role for the NRC and very hefty spending increases by the Government of Canada. Naturally, funding was not found to be anywhere near as much as was needed and the option was dropped. The third option, the low cost option, was not even realized by the NRC. The NRC did, however, receive budgetary increases from the previous Government in the last few years.
It can be said that the NRC engages in two different kinds of research although the distinction between basic research and applied research is often blurred. Scientists often say that basic research is pure scientific inquiry. Its results may never prove to have a commercial application and often a commercial application, if there is one, may take years to have effect on the economy. On the other hand, applied research, at least at the NRC, has a close relationship to industry. Basic research at the NRC has always been short changed, although Option 1 of the 1985 year plan would have greatly enhanced this endeavour. Applied research has for some time predominated at the NRC to the extent that some 90 per cent of its research activity has been closely tied with industry.
The second five-year plan being unveiled today will take the NRC even further down the path of industrial research at the expense of basic research. It is this trend that disturbs many Canadian scientists. As I said before, the plan is not that detailed in terms of numbers but one could quote from the plan the intentions of the council to go more and more down the path of more basic research.
No doubt private sector technological leaders will be very pleased. What happened to the Tory belief in the discipline of the market-place? It would seem that there are very few risks to be faced by these companies. The taxpayers will be picking up the tab. Will this be a replay of the old Liberal research and development tax credits about which members of this Government complained when they were in opposition?
By diminishing even more the role of basic research, can we expect the slack to be taken up elsewhere? Canadian universities have done much of the basic research in recent years and have done well despite a shortage of money. Many of those
November 27, 1985

universities have been struggling with cut-backs brought on by provincial Governments and by a federal Government determined to reduce its share of post-secondary funding. Some predict that basic research will suffer even more. Furthermore, Canada does not have outstanding research institutions whose research capabilities match those of MIT or CalTech.
In the 1980 five-year plan, the NRC dreamed of making a greater contribution to the world's pool of scientific knowledge. The thrust of the new five-year plan will not allow the NRC to be a greater contributor to this pool of knowledge. As the Council's President Mr. Kerwin, says, the NRC will not abandon its essential role of developing expertise for the nation by encouraging long-term research. What he does not say is that this role is already very small and we cannot expect it to grow.
I am sure many Members of the House know that Canada does less than 4 per cent of the scientific research and development in the world. With the budget restrictions and cut-backs, that percentage is shrinking at an ever-expanding rate.
One of the problems in not contributing to the pool of scientific knowledge is that Canada will be left further and further behind because of the cut-backs. We already purchase a considerable amount of technology developed elsewhere. One of the reasons for that is that so much of Canada's economy is foreign-owned. There are many branch plants in this country. If we do not enhance our basic research at a world class research station like the NRC, we will surely have to buy even more technology from elsewhere in the future. We should also worry about the brain drain. Many world class Canadian scientists may take their skills and experience to an environment that welcomes them and their families.
One should support applied research for the benefits it can deliver. Many jobs are created directly, and of course there is much spinoff. Canada's R and D performance is not exactly stalwart when compared to that of other countries. As noted before, the lack of emphasis on basic research support is shameful.
In conclusion, I would like to say that I do have a tremendous concern about the general cut-backs in the funds given to research and development and the trend lines one sees when looking back over the last number of years.

And in the R and D sector, Mr. Speaker, both private and public spending as a percentage of our Gross National Product has gone down. In 1981, for instance, 1.6 per cent of our GNP was spent on research and development. In 1985, this was 1.3 per cent, which means a drop from 1.6 to 1.3.
Federal participation is going down as well. Twenty years ago, between 1963 and 1967, 47 per cent of total funding in the R and D sector came from the federal Government. She said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak today on the second reading of Bill C-84, an Act to amend the Income Tax Act and related statutes. These include the Canada Pension Plan Act, the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, the Financial Administration Act and the Petroleum and Gas Revenue Act.
This Bill contains measures proposed in two notices of Ways and Means motions tabled in the House earlier this year, one a general Ways and Means motion tabled on May 23 and the other a detailed notice of a Ways and Means motion tabled on November 21.
The Bill represents a substantial and integral component of the Government's program to secure durable economic renewal for Canadians. Members will recall that we established the broad framework for that strategy in November of last year. Since then we have moved clearly and consistently to develop and implement specific initiatives-the building blocks for durable economic renewal.

The Bill represents a substantial and integral component of the Government's program to secure durable economic renewal for Canadians.
Members will recall that we established the broad framework for that strategy in November of last year. Since then we have moved clearly and consistently to develop and implement specific initiatives-the building blocks for durable economic renewal.

We know the policies of the Government are already bringing about very positive and encouraging results. For example, the inflation rate is the lowest since 1971. The prime rate is
November 27, 1985

down 3.6 per cent from where it was a year ago when we launched our initiatives for economic renewal. Also, bank rates and mortgage rates are at the lowest levels they have been in seven years. These indicators are indeed important building blocks in the Government's strategy to bring lasting economic prosperity to the people of the country.
I wish to point out to Members opposite that with interest rates at the levels I have just mentioned this means the average Canadian farmer or business person with liabilities of $100,000 will save $3,000 a year. With mortgage rates at today's levels, it means a young Canadian couple buying their very first home with a $50,000 mortgage will pay $8,000 less over a five-year term and save $125 per month.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
I might add that this young couple will have a far better chance of owning their first home because since the Government came to office a year ago I know the House will be pleased to note that new housing starts are up by almost 50 per cent.
The renewal strategy is designed to create steady and sustained improvement in the basic conditions for economic growth. This growth will be powered by the dynamism of the private sector and supported by a federal Government which recognizes not only its responsibilities but its proper limitations as an economic regulator and participant.
The Bill proposes to continue our strategy for far-reaching and wide-ranging economic renewal. Therefore, it is appropriate to review briefly the cornerstones of the strategy. First, the Government is determined to reduce the federal deficit and bring the growth of the public debt under control. By putting our fiscal house in order we are ensuring that the private sector has the scope for revitalized growth. I am pleased to report that our rigorous yet responsible efforts to date have made positive headway with the debt problem. We are presently seeing the slowest growth in Government spending in 17 years and apart from servicing the national debt Government spending is rising by only 2 per cent. The deficit is $500 million lower now than it was a year ago. This is an achievement which no Liberal Government could muster in the last 15 years.
The Government is cutting $4 billion this year, $6.1 billion next year and by 1990 the national debt will be $75 billion lower because we are working deligently to ensure Government works efficiently and without waste. We will continue to build on this success.
A second cornerstone of our renewal strategy is the direct encouragement of private initiative as the key to productive growth and job creation. Since we established our framework for economic renewal last November, we have also moved clearly and consistently to develop and implement specific initiatives that bring employment opportunities for Canadians. My colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald), has worked closely with our provinces and
Income Tax Act
with the private sector to develop a strategy of jobs for Canadians. We have seen the national unemployment rate decline 1.3 per cent and the youth unemployment rate drop by 2 per cent since September 1984, and we have seen 333,000 jobs created within the private sector since September 1984. Our policies and commitment are fostering higher investment, greater innovation, increased international competitiveness and a positive climate for the birth and growth of new enterprise. The clear signals we have given the private sector and initiatives we have taken to date have already borne fruit in the form of greater private sector activity and improving economic performance in almost all sectors of our economy.
Third, we are improving the efficiency and effectiveness of Government by cutting waste, by removing obstacles to economic growth and by making better use of scarce and precious resources. We are ensuring that Government assumes a less intrusive place in the lives of Canadians.
Finally, we are bringing about all these vital changes in a manner that is as fair as humanly possible. In acting to improve the climate in which our private sector in Canada can excel, we are building on the basic sense of compassion, tolerance and justice that is the essence and the character of our Canadian people. The Bill we are considering today is firmly and squarely based on three cornerstones of our economic renewal strategy.
The Bill will implement many significant measures that my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), introduced in this Government's first full Budget. These measures have attracted widespread support and are eagerly awaited by Canadians. The Bill that we are considering amends the Income Tax Act in significant ways. Measures contained in the Bill include: a lifetime $500,000 capital gains tax exemption for individuals-and that includes small capital gains as well; capital tax on larger financial institutions; modifications to the rules governing investment in small business by pension and other retirement income plans; rules to prevent taxpayers from splitting income among family members just to reduce tax; and changes to review Revenue Canada's powers to audit and examine taxpayers' books and records, including its powers of search and seizure. These measures touch on a wide variety of issues including tax fairness, fiscal responsibility, taxpayers' rights and efficiency of government programs.
I have indicated that this Bill provides for a maximum half-million dollar personal lifetime capital gains exemption. This is perhaps the most significant measure in this Bill and is one which changes both the direction and character of the Canadian tax system in a positive way. The capital gains exemption recognizes that the Canadian economy can be dynamic and productive when the successes Canadians achieve are rewarded.
Canada has been described as a nation of savers. With measures such as the lifetime personal capital gains exemption, Canada will, I believe, become known as a nation of aggressive entrepreneurs who reap the rewards of their success and hard work from a thriving and prosperous economy.

November 27, 1985
Income Tax Act
1 spoke also today of tax fairness. This Bill contains measures which will prevent the use of income-splitting trusts to gain tax advantage. It is high time that the tax law is amended to correct this defect which has allowed those most able to hire tax advisers to take advantage of the tax system. I am pleased to note, as well, that this Bill promotes fairness in the tax administration. New measures defining the powers of search and seizure will ensure that the administration of the tax law complies with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
We recognize that small business is the engine of economic growth. This Bill contains innovative measures allowing small businesses to tap into new sources of equity investment. These measures, which allow access by small businesses to funds of retirement savings plans and pension plans, will benefit both pension plan administrators and small businesses. They are progressive ideas whose time has come.
This Government recognizes as well the importance of consultations in developing and refining policy initiatives. As evidence of this, I would point to the announcements already made regarding adjustments to budget proposals. This Bill provides for these as well as other modifications made in the detailed Ways and Means motions tabled last week.
The May Budget proposed that, as a result of the introduction of the capital gains exemption, capital losses incurred after 1984 would be deductible only from future capital gains. This Bill, however, allows net capital losses realized before the May Budget to be deducted from other sources of income to the extent of $2,000 per year. This, in effect, continues the pre-Budget treatment for capital losses realized before the Budget.
The lifetime capital gains exemption is a generous measure and is intended to encourage risk-taking by Canadians. It is not intended to diminish the fairness of the tax system by allowing transactions which, in effect, convert normal income into capital gains. Accordingly, various specific anti-avoidance rules have been added. These rules will counter the conversion of business or property income into exempt capital gains and the conversion of corporate capital gains into exempt capital gains of individuals.
In addition, special rules have been introduced to prevent the flow of capital gains, through conduits such as mutual funds, to individuals, and to prevent taxpayers from deferring gains through option agreements so as to avoid the transitional phase-in of the capital gains exemption. A specific anti-avoidance provision has also been introduced to prevent the shifting of exempt capita! gains from one person to another through the use of stock dividends, generally in private family corporate arrangements.
Two modifications have been made to the May Budget proposals with respect to investment tax credits. First, 1 know that Hon. Members will welcome the fact that the Cape Breton investment tax credit rate has been increased from 50 per cent to 60 per cent. Second, those taxpayers who do contract work for other taxpayers will not be entitled to investment tax credits on their contract work effective for contracts after November 21, 1985. This will not in any way
affect research and development companies in Canada carrying on research and development work on their own account or through contractors. It will, however, stop the double claiming of incentives.
The May Budget proposed a capital tax to be levied on large financial institutions. To confine its application to the very largest banks and trust companies, the threshold for this tax has been increased to $300 million of capital employed in Canada.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, this Bill provides for a new direction for the Canadian income tax system. It provides for new measures such as the $500,000 lifetime maximum personal capital gains exemption to encourage small and medium size investors, small businessmen, farmers and all Canadians to invest their savings in productive economic activity and to take the risks that our business climate needs. The Bill also improves the fairness of the tax system by removing some of the unintended ways in which advantage may be taken of the system. Finally, this Bill removes the controversial scientific research tax credit and replaces it with a refundable mechanism which is less open to abuse but which will continue to encourage legitimate research and development.
This Bill increases the effectiveness of Government programs by reducing the basis for investment tax credits where other grants or assistance have been received or expenditures made. This Bill increases the fairness of the tax system by introducing change of control rules to prevent unacceptable sales of unused tax credits. These changes are long overdue and we know that Canadians share our objective and desire to improve the economy. We know Canadians are willing to share some of these burdens so that we all share in the triumphs and in the forthcoming prosperity.
I do want to share with you as well some of the comments that my colleague, the Minister of Finance and I have received since we introduced this Budget. We have been told that it was the most encouraging Budget in the past decade. Canadians have written and telephoned to tell us the measures to encourage investment in small and medium-sized business are good for them and good for Canada. Canadians wrote to say that the capital gains tax exemption is a clear message to invest.
This is a major Bill. It is a complex Bill. However, such complexity is unavoidable where measures such as those contained in the Bill affect the fundamental principles of our tax system and where we are unwinding some of the problems we faced in the tax system before. The new direction this Bill provides and the benefits Canadians will gain more than justify these changes. I recommend Bill C-84 to this House. I look forward to speedy passage of these measures because they are so instrumental to economic renewal and prosperity in this country.

She has the extraordinary gall to come in here and talk about putting our fiscal house in order.

Then we have the case of Genstar and others as well. All of this could add up, I suggest, to as much as $2 billion. Throw in another $2.8 billion for the banks and another $500 million for ice-breakers, and we have the kind of fiscal constraint which this Government pretends to be practising. It is too bad that the actions do not match the rhetoric.
Then the Minister tries to tell us about a capital gains exemption which will do all kinds of wonderful things. I see the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), here. I see the Hon. Member for Ontario (Mr. Fennell) here. I see a number of Members who know better but they will not say anything. They know it is one of the stupidest tax provisions to ever be introduced in the history of income tax legislation. This is true for so many reasons, technical and equitable, that it boggles the mind.
She talks about small business being able to tap new sources of funds. Yes, 1 believe that is important and I must say that I am pleased the Government at least sought to tap these sources of funds, things like RRSPs and pension plans. However, once again it is the wrong approach to try and induce plans to invest in Canadian small business in order to free up money to invest elsewhere.
Let me try to be constructive, Mr. Speaker. I threw those comments out because it is difficult to sit in my seat and listen to the stream of self-congratulations coming from the Minister. That being said, let us try this afternoon to put some of the partisanship behind us and invite Members of the House to

November 27, 1985
Income Tax Act
discharge their responsibilities to their constituents. We all want to have a better and more equitable tax system. We are all here to achieve that end.
We waited nine months for the Budget to appear. Now, we have waited almost six months for the tax Bill to appear. One would have hoped that the fundamental flaws in the Budget could have been addressed during the intervening period. Well, they have not been. Unfortunately, as we all know, you cannot make a silk purse from a sow's ear. Nevertheless, the Budget could have been dramatically improved through some sensible modifications in the Bill which the Minister put before us. That has not taken place. She did tell us, of course, that the tax credit in Cape Breton has been increased from 50 per cent to 60 per cent. If that is going to make a major difference in Cape Breton, so be it. I do not think it will make any contribution whatsoever.
In any event, the Budget was unfair. Members on all sides of the House recognize that. It widens the gap between the rich and the poor in the country. Well, Mr. Speaker, the Budget remains unfair. The Budget suggested that there would be complex provisions introduced into the Income Tax Act. We have seen complex provisions introduced into the Income Tax Act through this tax Bill. I am glad to see that we now have the wisdom of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazan-kowski) because I know he will be able to make a contribution to this discussion in Cabinet and in caucus to try to bring some common sense to this piece of legislation before it is too late.
Notwithstanding what the Minister has said, we know that the Budget is economically unsound. We on this side of the House are not alone in saying that. Economists are saying it and the Institute for Policy Analysis at the University of Toronto has said it. In fact, some of the internal departmental analyses which have leaked out in one manner or another have also said it. Most important of all, instead of sending a clear message, the message is very ambiguous. There is almost no coherent thread of thought running through the various measures found in the various statutes to which the Minister made reference. Everyone knows that this is a bad Budget and the Government now has to put its best face on it. Having retreated-thank God-on a number of issues, it does not now want to retreat any further. However, retreat it must, because if it does not retreat now it will have to retreat in the next Budget at a cost of much time and expense in the private sector as well as in the House, in committee, and in various Departments.
Tax, of course, is a very complicated matter. I confess to you, Mr. Speaker, that I wish the Liberal Government had done a lot more to improve the taxation system in the country. There was a tax reform initiative by a Conservative Government in 1962; the Carter Commission. The Liberal Government followed that. I was not here at the time that the tax reform Bill was introduced in 1971. Frankly, I thought that was a bad piece of legislation and I still think so. Now, instead of taking advantage of the golden opportunity of having 211 seats in the house to bring forward sensible tax reform and give Canadians the kind of coherent, fair and equitable tax
system which would contribute to economic growth and which they deserve, our tory friends are in the process of making the situation even worse.
I would like to refer to a statement made by the Carter Commission with respect to what a tax system should achieve. I would then like to measure certain components in the budget and in the tax bill against the system as described. Carter said:
A tax system can be judged from different points of view. Is the system fair? Does it contribute as much as possible to the growth and stability of the economy? Are the rights and liberty of the individual protected? Does it help strengthen the federation? These questions reflect not only the many facets of taxation but also what we believe to be the principal objectives that Canadians wish to realize through their tax system. They want equity, more goods and services, full employment without inflation, a free society and a strong, independent federation.
Although these words were written almost 20 years ago, I suggest that Canadians feel the same way about their tax system today as they did then. They have been hoping, somewhat futilely, for the kinds of changes that are essential to give them the tax system which they deserve.
Does this tax Bill contribute as much as possible to the growth and stability of the economy? The Budget extracts billions of dollars from consumers, ordinary men and women, middle and lower income Canadians. They are being asked to foot this tax Bill. Drawing upon the famous document which is the estimates of the Department of Finance, if we take out the tax loss from the capital gains tax exemption, of which the Minister and the Government appear to be so proud, we find that direct tax on persons in the year 1990-91 will have increased by $5.2 billion. Can anyone in any of the Parties which sit in the House suggest that this will contribute to the growth and stability of the economy? Add to that the indirect taxes. Again I am going to take out the oil export charge because I do not think it is appropriate. No one knows where that tax falls. If we take that out and add the additional fuel taxes which are to come into effect in January to help replace the revenue lost by backing off from the deindexation of Old Age Security, we find that an additional $4.6 billion will be paid. Excluding corporate taxes and other taxes which are passed on, direct taxes on persons and indirect taxes which individuals have to bear, all of which are regressive, will amount to a grand total of almost $10 billion by 1990-91. The Minister is telling us that that will contribute to the growth and stability of the economy. It certainly does not meet the test which was laid down by Carter in his statement delivered in 1967 which I read to you a moment ago.
The impact of these various taxes is only beginning to be understood. We know what the impact is likely to be in the construction industry. Is the Government listening to the construction industry? Is the Government paying attention to the impact that this may have on the housing starts of which the Minister is so proud? Does anyone know what is going to happen to the trucking industry when a tax is put on distance in the country, which tax must be borne by the receiver of produce, whether food or clothing?

That is a typical example, this time from the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Finance, of the failure to understand that the tax Bills have to be taken as a whole. There is no one tax Bill which can be read without another. I am coming to that point. If the Member will pay attention he may learn a little about the problems with the tax system, which problems he should be taking before his committee for study. The fact of the matter is that these are the numbers and the Minister says that this Budget will contribute to the growth and stability of the economy. I do not know if the Member was here for the Minister's speech. As Members may or may not know, there are three sources of taxation. There are taxes on income, which are normally progressive in this country. There are taxes on consumption which are inevitably regressive under our system. Those are the taxes to which I just referred. Finally, there are taxes on capital. In Canada, I believe we have never successfully found the appropriate balance between these three sources of taxes.
Of course, the mosts visible tax is on income. Taxes on consumption are much less visible and the Government has tried to get away with a great amount of apparently invisible taxation. Retail sales taxes are more visible because they are applied to the retail level.
The manufacturer's sales tax and the customs tariffs are regressive. They fall equally upon the rich consumer of goods and the poor consumer of goods. There will be a change in the capital tax because the threshold has been raised. However, I have often argued in the House that a capital tax applied to a corporation is not paid by the corporation. Since it must be paid by someone else, I am not sure in any of these cases where that tax will fall. That tax is levied under Part VI of the proposed Bill.
That brings me to the issue of transparency to which we must pay close attention. It is necessary for us to know who is actually stuck with the tax bill. For example, the Government has applied a sales tax to pet food in the Budget. That tax is to be borne by the pet owner. However, when a tax is put on the profits of a company which manufactures pet food, it may be borne in part by the pet owner, the shareholder and by the employees who receive less wages. The fact is that is has to be passed on somewhere. This is where the problem of less transparency arises especially with respect to corporate taxes which many people, especially my friends in the NDP, regard as some sort of panacea to taxation. However, corporations do not pay taxes. As a matter of fact, I have heard that when the United States Treasury hires new tax experts fresh from
Income Tax Act
university, the first question they are asked is who pays the corporate tax. If the person has an answer they are not hired.
Transparency of taxes is essential. I can go to any restaurant in Ottawa, Montreal or Toronto where people are dining in a luxurious restaurant. Who is paying the bill if it is tax deductible? Is it the partners, the shareholders or the Government? I suggest that nine times out of ten it is not the person dining. This introduces inflation into our system and makes many of the services unattainable by ordinary Canadians.
Canadians are tired of being screwed by the tax system. The Government is squandering its opportunity to do something about it. It has produced an inequitable Bill that is complex and simply builds on a system which is already inadequate. My friends opposite know that.

They know perfectly well this is a very bad Budget and that the Bill before the House is unsatisfactory. But they are going to vote for the Bill just the same because of the tradition of party discipline.

I am convinced that our electors including those represented by 211 Tory Members, roughly 75 per cent of the population or 18 million people, expect more from them than to simply stand up and vote for this Bill with all of its obvious flaws simply because the Minister of Finance and the Government do not want to reconsider this legislation. It makes a mockery of the process if we are trapped into an attempt to fight a Bill that has irresistible momentum because of 211 Members.
It is true that the Government backed off on the pension question last spring and reconsidered other matters, but it was not as a result of Members of the House who were able to bring pressure to bear on the Government. It was not as a result of what happened on the back-benches. The opposition, playing its role by raising the issues, had to have the support of Canadians. It was referred to by some as "grey power", when that group of Canadians came here to say that pension deindexation was unacceptable. When it became apparent that votes were at stake, the Government reacted. That is not what should happen. Common sense should make us react. We have enough collective brain power in the House of Commons to improve this legislation but I fear, having listened to the Minister, that it will be very difficult to make that change.
We were sent here to do a job for the people of Canada. I suggest that we cannot let this notion of party discipline allows us to railroad a piece of legislation through that is obviously as bad as this. While I do not believe Canadians have the respect they should for this place, how can they have that respect when they know that this is becoming a House of voting robots.

November 27, 1985
Income Tax Act
and I am not happy about all of the legislation that has gone through the House in the past, under whatever Government.
A committee has come forward with some good recommendations and I think the time has come for change. Canadians want a change. Canadians voted for change but it is not happening. All 211 Tory Members will get up to vote for this Bill which is so obviously wrong in so many respects. While portions of the Bill have been changed, much work remains to be done in order to have legislation which provides economic growth, equity and satisfies Canadians that parliamentarians are providing true input into legislation.
Let us use the capital gains tax provision as an example of what is wrong with this Bill. The Minister praised this provision, saying that it would encourage investment and so on. Beginning in 1985, Canadians will be exempt progressively from paying tax on $500,000 of capital gains over their lifetime. This provision was said to be designed especially with a view to encouraging investment in small-and medium-sized businesses. The Member for Mississauga South agrees with that, as do other Members of the House.
We have been told, and I agree from my own study of the matter, that jobs-
[ Translation]

So it makes very goods sense to try and attract investment to this sector.

That being said, what about the provision? The provision effectively applies to all capital property. There are a couple of exceptions with respect to employees' stock options and so on. We have heard that this capital property can include condominiums in Florida, yachts in the Caribbean, stamps, coins, jewellery, foreign securities or any assests on a world-wide basis. This is intended to encourage investment in the small and medium-sized business sector.
Mir. Gormley: Lots of farmers. Lots of fishermen.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext: The Member to my right is being provocative. I think that a little ad libbing and a little fun in the House is sometimes good.

The Minister has stated that people are excited about this formula and will invest. However, that is not what I hear.
