We know from statistics that 4 per cent of Canadian taxpayers have income in excess of $50,000. We also know that 63 per cent of all capital gains go to those people with $50,000 and over. There is no equity. It does not accomplish its purpose in terms of creating investment in the small and medium-sized business sector. What does it do, Mr. Speaker? It costs one hell of a lot of money, money that could be better spent elsewhere.
If we look again at the Department of Finance's numbers which, I understand, are probably being revised because they are understated, we see from this document that was released, leaked, whatever on or about budget night, that in 1985-86- by those conservative estimates-it was going to cost $300 million, next year $600 million and by 1990-91, $1.25 billion. I repeat for those members who are getting used to these big numbers being thrown around in their caucuses, $1.25 billion. I suppose $1.2 billion does not sound much beside $2.8 billion but it is a lot of money. I suggest too that that money is not going into any productive pursuits whatever. That money is being blown. Yet we hear at the same time the importance of deficit reduction, about the banks, the ice-breakers, the tax rulings, and here we have $1.25 billion blown by this provision in the Budget with no focus and no job creation that is guaranteed at all.
I said I would not go on long this afternoon because my colleagues will be following up themes in this Budget, if there are themes. There are certainly no coherent themes, but my colleague will be following up themes of waste, of complexity of inequity and so on.
I want to leave my fellow parliamentarians with one thought. I want to come back to it once again because I feel it is terribly important. I hope, I have always hoped, and I hope people in this Chamber share my hope that we will some day discharge those responsibilities which our electors have given to us here on the floor of the House of Commons. 1 do not think any of us can be satisfied we are discharging our responsibilities if we allow this tax Bill to pass in the form presented to us by the Minister.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I almost have tears in my eyes. I guess it is appropriate to have tears in one's eyes to rise on Bill C-84. We have 235 pages of revisions to the Income Tax Act of Canada. I do not know how many Members of Parliament have had an opportunity to look through these 235 pages. Quite frankly, I would be surprised if anyone has. Let us assume that two, three or five people in the House have actually sat down and attempted to go through this document.
We get into discussion in the hallways and in the coffee shops on Parliament Hill but it is time that we stop the nonsense of Bills containing 235 pages. Here we are discussing in principle Bill C-84, an Act to amend the Income Tax Act and Related Statutes, an Act to amend the Canada Pension Plan, the Unemployment Act, 1971, the Financial Administration Act and the Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act. We are amending all kinds of things in all kinds of ways and nobody knows what it is all about.
We have had a chance to look at some of the highlights. Normally if the Finance Department were serious about having Members of Parliament and others analyse what the Department is doing, it would have sent out an explanation
Income Tax Act
paper as it has in the past to explain what on earth all this legalese gobbledegook means.
The Government tabled an explanation document yesterday, but we are talking about 235 pages of tax changes. This is now like a tragic comedy. I think it is time, and I suspect Members of the House will agree, that we stop this. When we are dealing with such a complicated matter that has horrendous implications a Bill like this should be sent to the appropriate committee well in advance for discussion, so we can hear witnesses and experts in the various sectors. It should be analysed for a number of weeks, a number of months if necessary so we can understand what the Government of Canada is doing.
There are hundreds of Finance Department officials sitting somewhere in mystical offices near Parliament Hill, who, I guess, all year long with furled brows and pens, draft changes to the Income Tax Act based on suggestions by Members of Parliament, by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) and perhaps others. No one knows who these people are, what they are doing and why they are doing it.
Here in the last dying days before the Christmas recess we as parliamentarians are asked to rule and to decide on this incredible range of implications that will touch the lives of every Canadian for decades to come. It is not being done with proper analysis or with proper study. In fact it is not being done properly. Quite frankly, the process is totally unacceptable. I know the Government's Finance Committee Chairman will rise in his place shortly. I hope he will have something to say about this meaningless and silly process which is continually perpetuated year after year. It has to be changed, and that initiative for change has to come from the Government. It ought to come from the Minister of Finance, but I am not sure whether we have one any more. At least it could come from the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. I appeal to him to use his good offices in order to try to bring some sense into the process so that we can at least deal with this Bill as responsible and sensible parliamentarians, as opposed to being forced into this charade.
When we talk about changing the Income Tax Act of Canada, it has to be discussed within some kind of context. We will not simply be making a few changes to a few pages in the Act. There is a number of processes going on at the same time. Another set of tax regulations is also being changed in the excise tax Bill which is presently before the House.
The Government has decided in its wisdom that it should now place a special sales tax on all transactions which take place in the country. It wants to add another 1 per cent to the sales tax, one of the most regressive and punitive taxes which a country can have or a Government can impose. However, that is what the Government is doing. When one buys a set of winter tires, whether one is from a poor family or an extremely wealthy family, one pays the same sales tax. That is a very regressive, unfair, inappropriate, callous and uncaring action

November 27, 1985
Income Tax Act
to be taking. As well, there will be increased taxes on diesel fuel, aviation fuel and gasoline per se. As many Hon. Members have indicated over past days, it is really a tax on distance. It adds one cent per mile to the costs faced by truckers. Every commodity transported in the country will cost consumers more. The trucker or someone will have to take less profit. By and large it will be passed along to consumers. This discriminates against northern Canadians who have to fly in all their goods. With an increase in aviation fuel, it will cost them much more to live. Western Canadians who have to transport goods over vast distances will be paying more for their goods. It is discriminatory against them as well. The same could be said about people living in Atlantic Canada.
The Government decided to impose more taxes upon construction materials, affecting the people who build the country. They are the ones who build our houses and buildings. They create and leave clear evidence of what they contributed to society. Construction materials will be taxed.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext: It is already in difficulty.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext: Yes, that industry is already in difficulty. It provides employment and assists many other sectors, it is in difficulty at the present time, and now the Government is imposing a further levy.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext: We cannot get bricklayers in our community.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
I ask my hon. friend to travel to western Canada and ask about how healthy that industry is. He will get an ear full, because it is an industry which is on its knees today in western Canada. To impose a tax on construction materials is a very regressive step for the Government of Canada to take at this time.
Also the Government will impose taxes on pop, chocolate bars and all sorts of other confectionary items, as well as on dog food, cat food, canary food and goldfish food, and on pharmaceutical supplies. The list goes on and on, but I will not take up the valuable time of the House to indicate all the new taxes which will be imposed. That is the context within which we are discussing changes to the Income Tax Act today.
As a result of these taxes which I have just mentioned, as well as a few others, $2.5 billion per year will be extracted from the pockets of ordinary citizens and put into the coffers of Ottawa. Why is there this tax grab? Why is the Government so bloody desperate to cause hardship for the average Canadian household? Why does it want to bleed away $2.5 billion in increased excise taxes? I will tell the House why. If the Government bails out a bank for $1 billion, $2 billion or nearly $3 billion, if it gives a tax remission to Syncrude which might amount to $1 billion, if it gives another $1 billion to O&Y, if it makes a tax ruling on Genstar for tens of millions of dollars or perhaps more, and if it gives vast amounts of moneys to selective corporations, it has to come up with money from some place.
Therefore, the Government of Canada makes a desperate grab for money out of the pockets, wallets and purses of Canadians who can least afford any increase in taxation, let alone an increase on all these particular items. We will have to wait and see, but I know that those minions in the Department of Finance are drafting legislation for value added taxes. They have their forms put together. They have their papers drafted. They are talking to people across the country. We have been getting dribs and drabs of information in this regard. I do not know how many of us in the House care one hoot about giving serious consideration to a value added tax, which will result in billions and billions of extra tax dollars coming into the Ottawa Treasury from the taxpayers of Canada.
We do not really know what is going on. We do not know what finance people are doing in the back rooms, drafting up new ways of gouging the people of Canada. Government Members have to accept their responsibility. It is time that we pulled off the veils and opened up the doors of that place to find out what is going on in our tax system. I appeal to Hon. Members on the government benches to give the Finance Committee a special reference to look into the whole tax business and to stop perpetuating this continual hardship on people for questionable reasons and because of questionable motivation. What we are seeing here is really quite scandalous. There are incredible implications as the tax system is changed and altered. Quite frankly, there are some good changes. I have to be fair and responsible and say that there are some good tax changes, but most of them are not good. Most of the major boondoggles in the system do not appear here. They have not been touched; the Government has not laid a hand on them. By and large, this will make the Income Tax Act of Canada more biased, more unfair and less equitable than ever before. It will be biased in favour of certain wealthy Canadians and certain large corporations. That is what is being done. Let there be no doubt about it.
The problem is that our tax system is a voluntary compliance system. It relies upon Canadians being honest on their tax forms. It relies upon Canadians listing their incomes and paying a reasonable tax. However, when people are reminded day in and day out of the unfairness, bias and discriminatory aspects of the tax system, they lose faith. They have lost faith in the system, which consequently encourages more and more honest, law-abiding Canadians to seek out ways and means of avoiding or deferring tax.
Just this morning I read an article in the newspaper. I should like to refer to it for the particular benefit of Liberal colleagues to my right who brought in a tax loophole just before they left office whereby people could purchase luxury yachts and houseboats and almost get them free. It indicates that $165,000 can be deducted as a result of Canada's last great tax break, but that it has to be done quickly because it will finish by the end of December. It indicates that if one's annual taxable income is over $70,000-and that is a very select group of Canadians-one can deduct up to $165,000 over the next four years and own an income producing hard asset with 100 per cent borrowed funds. It goes on to indicate
November 27, 1985

all other advantages attached to buying a nice big yacht. We can thank the Liberals for introducing that loophole and thank the Minister of Finance for having the sense to close it off just after Christmas. There again, they can rush in and take advantage of that one.
I just noticed another little advertisement in this morning's paper. It talks about tax sheltered real estate here in the nation's capital. For a down payment in 1985, projected reduction in taxable income for the next number of years will total something in the neighbourhood of about $30,000 if one puts down $1,000 and arranges one's funds in a certain way. That is not a bad deal. These little notices have appeared in today's paper. In the next little while, they will start to flood into the newspapers as people adjust and become creative in their accounting before the year end in order to take advantage of all these loopholes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext: Are you going to get in on that one?

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
Perhaps you can get in on it before it is too late.
We do our best to remind people that there are still many, many Canadians who are upper-income earners or are wealthy and who year after year do not pay any income tax. They do not pay $1,000, $100, or $1, they pay no income tax year after year.
The other day, I received a letter from a constituent who said he was really interested in all this unfairness. He asked me to give him a list of all the loopholes these people used. He said that he was in the $100,000 per year bracket and wanted to know these things.
The other day, in a comment to an Ottawa Citizen reporter, a Revenue Canada official had this to say:
A Revenue Canada official said the deductions that allow high-income earners to pay no income tax are available to anyone in theory but in practice only to those who are able to "arrange their affairs" in the right way.
He went on to say that the 178 people earning more than $250,000 who paid no income tax used the following deductions: the dividend tax credit on 50 per cent of dividends paid by Canadian corporations, interest dividends and capital gains deductions, charitable donations, interest and carrying charges on borrowed investment funds, petroleum exploration venture investments and the Canadian motion picture film investment. They also claimed deductions for Canada Pension Plan and unemployment insurance contributions, Registered Pension Plans, et cetera. This gentleman was kind enough to list for this reporter's benefit some of the more obvious and popular loopholes that people who were making $250,000 per year were using to pay not one single penny in income tax.
Another group composed of 176 Canadians made $100,000 in the last tax year. They paid no income tax, not one single penny. There were more than 8,000 people whose income was in excess of $50,000 per year who paid no income tax. The numbers are getting larger and larger each year. I have been commenting on this for nearly six years. At first the numbers were small and I was just making the point that we needed
Income Tax Act
some kind of change to the tax system. The situation is getting more interesting and more unbelievable as the years pass. Every year the numbers are infalted. Why is this? Because more and more loopholes are provided in the tax system. More and more opportunities for those who can use creative accounting techniques are now available in the tax system.
As we perpetuate a system that is now understood by everyone to be grossly unfair, biased and discriminatory against ordinary Canadians, more and more people do not pay taxes at all. Ordinary law abiding Canadians decide that if everyone else is taking advantage of loopholes of which they cannot take advantage, they will do a little bartering and will use cash for transactions. The tax man will not know about that. More and more of the economy moves underground all the time. People estimate that between $30 billion and $50 billion worth of transactions per year are operating underground, unknown to the tax man. This means that the entire tax system begins to crumble. If ordinary Canadians have no faith in the tax system, it bodes very poorly for the future of Canada.
Ordinary Canadians look not only at the upper-income earners who do not pay tax but at those incredibly large corporate citizens. The small business people, the farmers, the fishermen and the corner store operators are struglling just to make ends meet these days.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext: How many farmers paid income tax?

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
Farmers as well. They pay all of the taxes. They have to fill out all of the forms and even collect taxes in areas which impose sales taxes. Then these ordinary Canadians read articles hidden in the back pages of the newspapers indicating that companies like the Royal Bank of Canada, the Bank of Montreal, Shell Oil, Hudson's Bay and Genstar, companies that are making profits in the hundreds of millions of dollars, pay no corporate income tax at all. These companies are not so fortunate year after year. Sometimes they get caught out and have to pay a little bit in corporate income tax. When those companies pay no income tax in certain years while the struggling entrepreneur pays every year, something is desperately wrong with our system.
The other day, a friend of mine, a rancher, and 1 were sitting in a restaurant. It was not a fancy restaurant but more of a run of the mill restaurant. A number of business people were sitting at the table beside us. Both tables finished at about the same time and we were both deciding who should pay for the cheque. We overheard the conversation at the next table. One of them said: "I'll take the cheque, don't worry. It will go on my expense account". What is available to a certain select group of people in society is not necessarily available to others. I am not saying that that is not good. I am simply saying that it discriminates against the people who work in certain kinds of occupations.
Shucks, let us move right into the capital gains tax area. When Carter held a tax commission a few years ago, he said that it was time we called a buck a buck. He said that if we make a dollar, we should pay a fair tax on that dollar. This

November 27, 1985
Income Tax Act
Government does not believe in that philosophy, it believes that the system should treat differently those folks who make money as a result of obtaining capital gains. That would include people who sell condominiums in Maui, buy and sell luxury yachts in the Caribbean or do other interesting things outside of Canada. If those people make money from those transactions, they do not pay any income tax whatsoever. Why on earth does the Government think this is a great bloody idea? The Government tells those who make money through investments and receive capital gains by doing work outside the country that they do not have to pay any income tax at all and that over the years they can accumulate up to $500,000. What does it tell the poor guy who is on the fish boat, the person in the coal mine and the person struggling to make a living when they find out that these folks do not pay any income tax because they have white collar jobs?
For certain areas of agriculture, the capital gains tax exemption makes sense. It makes sense for certain small businesses. I will listen carefully to my friend, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) who will speak next. I will ask him to do me the favour of explaining why someone who is selling a condominium in Jamaica, Miami or Maui should not pay income tax on the money he or she derives from that transaction. I for the life of me cannot figure that out.
If the Government is interested in helping Canadians and wants to have a capital gains tax exemption, why should it not at least restrict it to operations within Canada? If we are interested in creating jobs and helping people to reinvest, let us at least ask people to reinvest in our own country. I will be looking forward to hearing my friend explain that one a little later.
We have a system which treats certain kinds of income differently from other kinds of income. If that is not discriminatory, I do not know what is. That is like saying we will immediately favour people who derive their incomes from selling dividends, or from capital gains, or whatever, and we will discriminate against the people who are the real hard working Canadians who normally pay their taxes at source. It is a very unfair situation. I suppose the Minister of Finance is living out his goal. Not many months ago in a speech to the Canadian Economics Association in Montreal he said: "No matter how we define the term Canada has an acute shortage of rich people." He is doing his best to assist those who are nearly there by bringing in a whole new set of tax loopholes which will again assist the very wealthy in our country.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext: He wants to make more poor ones rich. He wants to build up the poor; you want to tear down the rich.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
One of the things the Government has held up as a major initiative is with respect to capital gains exemptions. I wish to remind my hon. friend opposite that when we look at the number of tax Filers, let us say in the $50,000 range, they amount to a very small percentage of all taxpayers. Yet, they account for nearly 65 per cent of the total benefits accruing
under the capital gains provision. It is clear that this particular item which the Government holds up as a major initiative will help a select number of Canadians. Of course, it will cost us. In other words, when one does not pay tax on capital gains it will cost the people of Canada. It will cost the people of Canada $1 billion over the next two years. That is contained in the Government's own fiscal plan. We know who will make up the difference. I know that you are a very knowledgeable and wise man, Mr. Speaker, and that you know when these folks are not paying their $1 billion that the ordinary Canadian must pay more than they should to make up the difference. Yes, they sell Texas oil wells and condos in Maui.
There is something good in the tax paper, that is, the proposal to allow a tax credit of $700 to accrue to an individual investing in a labour-sponsored venture capital organization. It is designed to assist small and medium-sized businesses. That is a positive initiative. Some 20 per cent or $700, which ever is less, will be allowed as a tax credit. That is an encouraging development, particularly with respect to the development of venture capital.
I do have some concerns with the Bill. I am concerned about the increase in the Registered Retirement Savings Plan and the registered pension plan regarding non-taxable contribution limits. The new limits will be increased to $7,500 next year, $9,500 the year after, $11,500 the year after that, and up to $15,500 by the year 1990. What does this mean? It means that if a person has $15,000 in loose change at the end of the year he can put it into a retirement pension plan and not pay any tax on it. I ask Hon. Members: How many people at the end of the year end up with $15,000 in change which they can invest in a retirement pension plan? That is what is provided here. How many people can really take advantage of this great provision? Quite frankly, the people who will take advantage of it are those people who do not need it.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext: Small-businessmen and women.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
I do not know many small-businessmen in my constituency who have $15,000 lying around which they can invest directly into retirement savings plans at this point in time.
I would like to consider a few other aspects of the Bill. Today, we are just talking about the principle of the Bill; we are not getting into a thorough point-by-point analysis of the Bill. That will come somewhat later. There is a proposal with respect to investment in small business by pension plans. The proposal is that pension funds be allowed to establish small business investment corporations to direct funds into the small business sector. Let us consider the definition of the small business sector. I see that the Minister of State for Small Businesses (Mr. Bissonnette) is in the House. A small business is defined as a company with assets up to $35 million. That is a fairly small company! I do not know if these are the types of companies which really need assistance at this point in time. They have other sources of capital upon which they can draw, ample sources. The family-structured businesses, the very small businesses which are trying to open up new areas, new
November 27, 1985

ventures and which are trying new ideas will not qualify. There are some difficulties with respect to the Bill. It states that as an incentive pension funds will be allowed to invest $3 outside of Canada for every $1 which is invested in this type of venture. That is a peculiar way to show a commitment to assisting and developing activity here in our own country.
1 now wish to tak about the deindexing of personal exemptions and tax brackets. We know what happened when the Government tried this same thing on OAS. It saw the illogic of such an approach and it backed off. I am pleased the Government did that. However, it is now going to eliminate the full indexation for the basic personal exemption on the tax form and the personal tax brackets. These exemptions will trip in only for increases above 3 per cent. What this means is that individuals will be paying more tax each year. They will not be able to deduct as much from their taxable incomes as their incomes increase from year to year. They will be pushed into higher tax brackets, even if their real income does not change a bit. This will cost Canadians about $650 million. Who are these taxpayers? These are ordinary Canadians who will, once again, have to pay an extra $650 million over the next two years as a result of this deindexation proposal.
The $50 tax reduction used to reduce taxable income has been eliminated. That is another $600 million out of the taxpayers' pockets. The ones who will feel this most acutely, and let there be no question about it, will be the low and middle-income Canadians. They will be the ones who will feel this proposal. If a person is in the $200,000 a year bracket he will not worry much about his ability to deduct $50 off his taxable income.
I would now like to deal with the temporary surtax on upper income earners. When one looks at all of the so-called fairness provisions introduced by the Minister today one will see that they are all temporary. All of the ones which will hit normal, ordinary middle and low-income Canadians are permanent. However, the corporate changes, the 5 per cent corporate surtax, that is temporary. It will be off in a few months. The temporary tax on the large financial institutions is a temporary tax. I am sure they will have trouble affording that 1 per cent!
There is a provision for the extension of the Small Business Bond Program. It was a nice gesture. I have yet to find a single person who has ever found a small business bond out there. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Budget measures in Bill C-84 include some which can be readily supported. For example, there is some modest assistance to the
Income Tax Act
disabled, coming from the groundwork of the last Parliament's special committee on the disabled and handicapped. There is also assistance to artists, again based on recommendations of a committee that sat in the last Parliament, the subcommittee on taxation of visual performing artists and writers.
However, these are overshadowed by two poorly conceived and patently unfair Budget measures. The $500,000 lifetime capital gains tax exemption will reward a wealthy minority without any requirement for benefit to the Canadian economy while the deindexation of the personal income tax system will take progressively larger tax bites from low and middle income earners who are least able to afford it.
The capital gains tax exemption is a no-strings gift, with 63 per cent of the benefit going to the 4 per cent of Canadian taxpayers earning over $50,000 a year. The measure is complex and cumbersome to administer and, despite the Government's assumption, there is no evidence that Canadian businesses will benefit since any investment anywhere in the world qualifies for the exemption. There is no requirement that it create one single Canadian job.
On the other hand, the deindexation of the Canadian personal income tax system means a steep tax increase for the majority of Canadians who cannot afford to invest much of anything. Over the next four years, those with an annual income of $15,000 will have a cumulative tax increase of 36 per cent, while those earning $100,000 a year will have an increase of only 4 per cent. Deindexation, coupled with the Budget's move to increase sales and excise taxes on a wide range of consumer goods, puts an inordinately heavy burden on low and middle income earners. They are the very people who would strengthen economic growth through consumer spending were it not for the dampening effect of these inequitable proposals.
What deindexation means is that full indexation of the basic personal tax exemption, set at $4,140 for this year, is to be ended. Instead of keeping pace with inflation, the basic exemption will be indexed only to increases in the consumer price index exceeding 3 per cent. Of course, this effectively amounts to a tax increase because as a person's exemptions decrease, the taxable income increases and he or she is pushed into higher tax brackets. Therefore, a person on a fixed income or whose salary remains virtually unchanged will pay more and more tax due to deindexation of the personal tax exemption.
Deindexation has been described by some as a sneaky and clandestine tax increase. The language may sound harsh, but I fear that it is accurate. The sneaky aspect of this measure comes with the cumulative effect it will have. In its first year, deindexation of the personal tax exemption is expected to yield $570 million. However, by 1990-91, it will extract eight times this amount, or $4.4 billion from taxpayers. This amount will be extracted mainly from low and middle-income earners because the affluent will be able to use the capital gains tax exemption to reduce their personal taxes.
There is a double whammy effect for taxpayers from the deindexation. Since provincial personal income taxes are a percentage of the federal basic income tax, Canadians will end

November 27, 1985
Income Tax Act
up paying more provincial taxes. For every extra $2 Ottawa collects, the provinces will get $ 1. The combined federal-provincial personal income tax increase in 1990-91 will exceed $4.8 billion. Deindexation will also have the effect of adding on to the income tax rolls, those people who are not currently paying tax because their incomes are too low. If their incomes manage to keep pace with inflation while exemptions and tax brackets remain stable, they will find themselves having to pay income tax.
For those individuals and families of modest means, the deindexation proposal is harsh. Clearly, the Government knows this. The Budget did not contain any long-term projections of the billions of dollars it expects to get through deindexation, although such forecasting is a normal part of all Budget planning and is normally available in Budget documents. However, it was not available in this Budget.
The Government was not proud of what it was doing and was not prepared to be open with taxpayers about the cost five years from now. However, the insidious effect of deindexation is such that by 1990, a family earning $15,000 a year will pay 36 per cent more in taxes. A family with a total income of $30,000 annually will have by 1990 a 16 per cent increase while the minority with $100,000 annual income will have an increase of only 4 per cent.
Another measure that has been called unfair and sneaky is the elimination of the $50 tax reduction as of the 1986 tax year. This was a tax break that primarily benefited low and middle income earners for whom $50 is not a small sum. Eliminating it will bring the Government $650 million. Singles with annual incomes under $30,000 will pay $50 more tax, while couples with incomes under $40,000 will pay $100 more tax.
In sharp contrast to these measures, which whittle away small amounts from each of the large number of low and middle-income Canadians, is the generous treatment given to the affluent by means of the capital gains tax exemption. The Budget proposes a change in capital gains exemption so as to give individuals a lifetime tax exemption of $500,000 for gains realized after 1984. The Government's stated hope is that this measure will encourage investment in Canadian businesses. There are no requirements to enforce that in the Bill before us.
The capital gains tax exemption will be an important influence on who pays and who benefits from the tax measures in the Budget. Starting at an income level of $50,000, the income tax load begins to diminish considerably because of the capital gains tax exemption. Obviously it is affluent Canadians who are best able to take advantage of this tax break and to plan their affairs so as to take advantage of it. The affluent are a minority in Canada. Based on 1982 statistics, only 4 per cent of Canadians have incomes of $50,000 or more, yet about 63 per cent of the benefits of the capital gains tax exemption can be expected to accrue to this 4 per cent. Capital gains tax exemption is expected to save investors $ 1.25 billion a year by 1990. It means that Canada will tax its wealthy more lightly
than any other industrialized country. Affluent Canadians will be paying for the same increases in sales tax, excise tax and deindexation as low and middle-income earners, but the affluent will have the option of offsetting this many times over through the capital gains tax exemption.
The capital gains tax exemption clearly favours the affluent on the assumption that their investment will contribute to economic growth. I repeat, Mr. Speaker, there is no evidence that this will happen. The capital gains tax exemption is not targeted to Canadian investment. In fact, it is completely open. There is no requirement that it create a single Canadian job. Not only is this proposal unfair to the majority of Canadian taxpayers, but it makes no sense economically.
In the six months since the Budget was introduced, the Government seems to have quailed in the face of criticisms of the proposed capital gains tax exemption. The Government has remained silent on the issue, failing to produce any further information for practitioners in the financial community. The latter says the measure is complex, cumbersome to administer, an interesting observation that reminds us the proposal came from a Government that promised tax simplification.
We will not consolidate economic recovery or promote growth without consumer demand. I suggest that business needs customers more than it needs tax incentives, but prospects for a consumer-led recovery are seriously impaired by this Budget.
The heavy burden imposed by this Budget's tax increases and deindexation will drastically reduce consumer expenditure. Low and middle-income earners, who have to spend most of their disposable income on the necessities of life, will have less to spend because they will be paying more in taxes. These Budget measures are not such as to create a favourable climate for economic growth. Regressive tax and expenditure measures will take billions out of the economy, out of consumers pockets at a time when consumption is key to sustaining economic recovery.
In 1990, Budget measures will extract over $4 billion in income tax, over $2.6 billion in sales and excise taxes. The Government appears to be banking heavily on a rise in confidence to spur economic growth yet the Budget measures do little to help and a great deal to hurt confidence.
Taxpayers were promised a tough but fair Budget. If a family of four with a $20,000 income loses over $900 by 1990 due to the many taxes and reduced inflation protection imposed by this Budget, that is tough for families, but is it fair? If three-quarters of a million Canadians fall below the poverty line by 1990, that is tough for disadvantaged Canadians, but is it fair?
It is no wonder that confidence is wanting when the Government promised fairness and then proceeds to implement a barrage of new taxes, increasing taxes while stripping protection against inflation from low and middle-income earners, the very people who would otherwise because of their large number be at the forefront of a consumer-led recovery.
November 27, 1985

The prospects for economic growth out of this Budget are not encouraging. This is bad news for the unemployed who have been waiting a long time for the jobs, jobs, jobs to materialize. There has been some job creation in the last year, but mainly part-time jobs without standard pay and benefits. There has not been a concomitant increase in permanent full-time jobs. I was rather pleased to hear the Hon. Member for Kam-loops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) indicate that part of today's Bill dealt with changes to the family benefit package. Bill C-84 contains the other two parts of the family allowance package. This Bill provides for the increase in the Child Tax Credits. It will increase the current 1985 base of $384 per year to $454 per year in 1986, $489 per year in 1987 and $524 per year in 1988. All of those increases to the Child Tax Credit provision apply to people who earn incomes under $23,500 per year and, of course, the increases are reduced as one's income climbs.

The third part of this over-all package of family benefit changes is also contained in this Bill, and that is the child tax exemption. This Bill reduces the child tax exemptions in the Income Tax Act. They will stay constant in 1985-86 at $710; in 1987 they will go down to $560 and in 1988 they will go down to $470 for families with children under the age of 18.
The combined effect of the changes to the family allowance system, the changes in the Child Tax Credit and the changes in the child tax exemptions under the Income Tax Act will be that lower income families will receive higher family benefits than families with higher incomes. That is a change from the situation as it exists right now. At this time, a family with an income of $30,000 per year gets more benefits under the three-part family benefit package than a family earning only $10,000 per year. All of these provisions were aimed at stimulating the economy. They go hand-in-hand with the provisions of the Bill, provisions such as the capital gains tax exemption. These provisions will allow pension funds to invest in small businesses.
All in all, there are three very beneficial provisions in this legislation to which members of the Opposition have not referred at all this afternoon. This Bill is an Income Tax Act amendment. However, we all know that there are provisions in the Bill which will increase taxes. Nobody likes to see taxes increase-not you, Mr. Speaker, and not any Member of the House. Certainly, no one across the country likes to see taxes increased.
However, at the same time, Canadians are realists. They realize that when there is a deficit of some $35 billion in the current fiscal year someone has to pay for it. As well, they realize that if they are earning 65 cents a week and they spend $1 a week they have to go out and borrow the extra 35 cents. When they realize that part of that 35 cents, in fact about 23 cents, is being spent to pay for the interest on money they have borrowed in order to spend that extra $1 each week they realize that cannot go on for very long. It cannot go on for long
in their own households, just as it cannot go on for long in the country. So they are realistic enough to know that tax increases provided for in this Bill will benefit them, their children and their grandchildren, whether they like and enjoy the tax increases or not. They do not, and we understand that.
The Bill really has three provisions, as far as 1 am concerned, which the people of Canada are looking for in a Bill dealing with income tax. The first is the provision of fairness to low income earners. I am referring to the provisions relating to family benefits, changes to the child tax credits, changes to child tax exemptions under the Income Tax Act and changes to the Family Allowance Act. All of these changes create more fairness for low income people in the country.
They are looking as well for fairness for middle income people. They want to make sure that there is going to be a fair tax system in place with no loophole from which other people can benefit and they cannot. This Bill does just that. It closes up some of those tax loopholes, eliminating the whole question of income splitting. They are also looking forward to the minimum tax law provisions which we expect to have in about two weeks' time. This Bill does provide fairness to middle income families. It does create a fairer tax system than we have had before.
Finally, Canadians are looking for an Income Tax Act which will help to stimulate the economy and create jobs, and that also is right here in this Bill. This Bill contains the three main features for which Canadians are looking and I hope that the House will consider it quickly and pass it before the Christmas break.
